plan: Natural-science passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000005) on competing explanations for ice's slipperiness; items emphasize evaluating explanations, a NOT-detail stem, and an evidence-weighing integration item.

passages.title: Why Ice Is Slippery
passages.text:
Ask most people why ice is slippery and they will offer an explanation they probably learned in school: the weight of a skater presses on the ice, the pressure melts a thin film of water, and the blade glides on that film. The account is tidy, memorable, and, according to most physicists who have checked the numbers, largely wrong.

Pressure does lower the temperature at which ice melts, but only slightly. Even the narrow blade of a skate, concentrating a person's full weight on a sliver of steel, lowers the melting point by only a few degrees at most. That might matter on a mild afternoon, when the ice is already close to melting. It cannot explain why people slip on sidewalks at fifteen degrees below zero, or why a stationary shoe, pressing far less sharply than a blade, slides just as readily.

A second explanation shifts attention from pressure to motion. When an object slides across ice, friction generates heat, and that heat may melt a thin layer of water at the point of contact. Experiments have supported this idea for fast-moving objects such as skates and sled runners. But friction requires movement, and ice is slippery even at the very first instant of a step, before any appreciable heat could build up.

The explanation that has gained the most support in recent decades was first suggested in the 1850s by the physicist Michael Faraday. Faraday proposed that the surface of ice is never entirely solid. The molecules in the outermost layer, he reasoned, have fewer neighbors to hold them in place than molecules deeper inside, and so they remain loosely bound, behaving more like a liquid than a solid even well below the freezing point. Modern measurements have detected such a layer, though researchers still debate how thick it is, how liquid-like it really is, and how it changes with temperature.

None of this means that pressure and friction play no role. On a rink, all three effects may operate at once, and their relative importance likely shifts with temperature, speed, and the materials involved. What has changed is the order of the story. The surface of ice, it turns out, is slippery before anyone steps on it.

candidates.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

choices.A: argue that pressure and friction play no part in making ice slippery.
choices.B: describe the experiments in which Faraday detected a liquid-like layer on ice.
choices.C: compare how slippery ice is on cold sidewalks and on indoor skating rinks.
choices.D: explain how competing explanations for ice's slipperiness have been tested and revised.

candidates.evidence: What has changed is the order of the story.
candidates.explanation: The passage moves through the pressure explanation, the friction explanation and Faraday's surface-layer explanation, showing the weaknesses of the first two and why the third has gained support.

A.rationale: Paragraph 5 says "None of this means that pressure and friction play no role."

B.rationale: Faraday proposed the layer; modern measurements detected it.

C.rationale: Sidewalks and rinks appear only as examples within the larger argument.

hints: Which choice covers all of them?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the passage in one sentence first.

candidates.remember: A main-purpose answer must fit every paragraph.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, which observation can the pressure explanation NOT account for?

choices.A: A shoe that is not moving slides as readily as a skate blade does.
choices.B: Skates glide more easily on ice that is already close to melting.
choices.C: Friction heats the surface of ice beneath fast-moving sled runners.
choices.D: The melting point of ice drops slightly as pressure on it increases.

candidates.evidence: or why a stationary shoe, pressing far less sharply than a blade, slides just as readily
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists two things the pressure explanation cannot explain: slipping at fifteen degrees below zero and a stationary shoe sliding as readily as a blade.

B.rationale: The passage says pressure "might matter" in that case, so the explanation can account for it.

C.rationale: This is part of the friction explanation, not something the pressure explanation is said to miss.

D.rationale: This is the fact the pressure explanation is built on.

hints: Find the sentence beginning "It cannot explain."

strategy.explanation: Locate the paragraph that tests the pressure explanation.

candidates.remember: Watch for NOT in the stem.

candidates.stem: The author's main objection to the friction explanation in paragraph 3 is that it:

choices.A: has never been supported by any experiment on ice.
choices.B: applies only at temperatures far below the freezing point.
choices.C: cannot account for slipperiness at the very start of a step.
choices.D: relies on pressure, which was already shown to be too weak.

candidates.evidence: ice is slippery even at the very first instant of a step, before any appreciable heat could build up
candidates.explanation: Friction needs motion to generate heat, but ice is slippery at the first instant of a step, before heat could build up.

A.rationale: Paragraph 3 says experiments support it for fast-moving objects.

B.rationale: The passage links friction to motion, not to a temperature range.

D.rationale: Friction depends on motion and heat, not on pressure.

candidates.remember: Look for the contrast word to find an objection.

candidates.stem: The author describes the school explanation as "tidy, memorable" (paragraph 1) primarily to:

choices.A: praise the explanation as a model of careful scientific reasoning.
choices.B: indicate that the explanation is correct but merely incomplete.
choices.C: show that physicists have not yet tested the explanation carefully.
choices.D: suggest why the explanation is widely believed even though it is largely wrong.

candidates.evidence: The account is tidy, memorable, and, according to most physicists who have checked the numbers, largely wrong.
candidates.explanation: The appealing qualities (tidy, memorable) explain why most people offer this explanation, and they set up the turn to "largely wrong."

A.rationale: The same sentence calls the explanation "largely wrong."

B.rationale: The author says it is "largely wrong," not just incomplete.

hints: Read the whole sentence, not just the two words.

strategy.explanation: Ask how the phrase relates to the rest of its sentence.

candidates.remember: Praise followed by a reversal sets up a correction.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 5, the word "order" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: The surface of ice, it turns out, is slippery before anyone steps on it.
candidates.explanation: The next sentence explains the change: slipperiness comes before the step, not after it. "Order" means the sequence of cause and effect.

A.rationale: A command does not fit "the order of the story."

B.rationale: The point is which comes first, not neatness.

hints: What does the next sentence say comes first?

strategy.explanation: Use the sentence after the word to define it.

candidates.remember: Context, not the common meaning, decides.

candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support Faraday's explanation over the friction explanation?

choices.A: A skate blade slides faster as it warms the ice directly beneath it.
choices.B: An object resting on ice begins sliding easily before any measurable heating occurs.
choices.C: Ice becomes more slippery as the weight pressing on it increases.
choices.D: Ice melts at a slightly lower temperature high in the mountains.

candidates.evidence: and so they remain loosely bound, behaving more like a liquid than a solid even well below the freezing point
candidates.explanation: Friction requires motion and heat; Faraday's layer exists before any motion. Easy sliding before any heating fits Faraday and contradicts what friction would require.

A.rationale: Heating that increases sliding supports the friction explanation.

C.rationale: This bears on the pressure explanation, not on Faraday versus friction.

D.rationale: This is unrelated to how the ice surface behaves.

hints: What does friction need that Faraday's layer does not?

strategy.explanation: For each finding, ask which explanation it favors.

candidates.remember: To favor one explanation, find what only it predicts.

candidates.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred from paragraph 4 that molecules deep inside a block of ice:

choices.A: remain liquid-like even well below the freezing point.
choices.B: were measured directly by Faraday in the 1850s.
choices.C: are held more firmly in place than molecules at the surface.
choices.D: move more freely as pressure on the ice increases.

candidates.evidence: have fewer neighbors to hold them in place than molecules deeper inside
candidates.explanation: Surface molecules have fewer neighbors holding them, so deeper molecules, with more neighbors, are held more firmly.

A.rationale: The passage says this of the outermost layer, not the interior.

B.rationale: Faraday reasoned about the molecules; measurements came later.

D.rationale: The passage says nothing about pressure affecting interior molecules.

hints: What do surface molecules have fewer of?

strategy.explanation: Reverse the description of surface molecules.

candidates.stem: The last paragraph mainly serves to:

choices.A: reject all of the explanations discussed earlier in the passage.
choices.B: allow that several effects may contribute while restating the central point.
choices.C: introduce a new explanation that combines pressure with friction.
choices.D: describe an experiment that finally settled the debate about ice.

candidates.evidence: None of this means that pressure and friction play no role.
candidates.explanation: It concedes that all three effects may act together, then restates the main point: ice is slippery before anyone steps on it.

A.rationale: It says pressure and friction may still play a role.

D.rationale: No experiment is described, and the passage says debate continues.

hints: What does the first sentence of the paragraph concede?
What does the last sentence repeat?

strategy.explanation: Describe the paragraph's two moves, then match.

candidates.remember: Concluding paragraphs often concede, then restate.

candidates.stem: The passage suggests that the pressure explanation would be most plausible for:

choices.A: ice that is already close to its melting point.
choices.B: ice at fifteen degrees below zero.
choices.C: a person standing still in ordinary shoes.
choices.D: the first instant of a step on a cold sidewalk.

candidates.evidence: That might matter on a mild afternoon, when the ice is already close to melting.
candidates.explanation: Because pressure lowers the melting point by only a few degrees, it could matter only when the ice is within a few degrees of melting.

B.rationale: The author says pressure "cannot explain" slipping at that temperature.

C.rationale: A stationary shoe presses "far less sharply," so pressure is even less able to explain it.

D.rationale: This is where the passage says the other explanations fail, not where pressure works.

hints: When does the author say pressure "might matter"?

strategy.explanation: Find where the author concedes pressure could work.

candidates.remember: A small effect matters only near the threshold.

candidates.stem: The author's attitude toward current research on the liquid-like surface layer is best described as:

choices.A: dismissive, because the thickness of the layer is still uncertain.
choices.B: doubtful that the layer could ever be measured by any method.
choices.C: certain that it fully explains how ice behaves in every setting.
choices.D: confident that the layer exists but aware of unresolved questions about it.

candidates.evidence: Modern measurements have detected such a layer, though researchers still debate how thick it is
candidates.explanation: The author states the layer has been detected (confidence) and notes ongoing debate about its thickness and behavior (open questions).

A.rationale: The author presents the layer as the best-supported explanation.

B.rationale: The passage says modern measurements have detected it.

C.rationale: Paragraph 5 says pressure and friction may also contribute.

strategy.explanation: Eliminate attitudes that are too extreme in either direction.

candidates.remember: Scientific writers often pair confidence with caveats.
